examples: It was walled in by precipices on the far side as well as on their own, and it was green and sunless, full of rapids and waterfalls.

examples: The Knight was seated in a curious silver chair, to which he was bound by his ankles, his knees, his elbows, his wrists, and his waist.

paragraphs.context: Nobody asked you to come barging in, did they?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jill is angry because Scrubb starts to tell her what to do. She says rude things to him.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Oh, go away and mind your own business,’ she said. ‘Nobody asked you to come barging in, did they? And you are a nice person to start telling us all what we ought to do, are you not? I suppose you mean we ought to spend all our time being nice to Them, and trying to please Them, and waiting on Them like you do.’

paragraphs.context: Jill was one of those lucky people who have a good head for heights
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jill is not afraid of high places. She is angry when Scrubb pulls her back, but then she sees how white his face is, and she looks down on him.
paragraphs.simple: Jill was one of those lucky people who are not afraid of high places. She did not mind at all standing at the edge of a very steep drop. She was rather angry with Scrubb for pulling her back. ‘Just as if I was a kid,’ she said. She pulled her hand out of his. Then she saw how very white his face had turned. She had no respect for him.

paragraphs.context: Crying is all right in its way while it lasts
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jill stops crying and finds that she needs water very much. She hears a small sound that might be water.
paragraphs.simple: Crying is all right for a time, while it lasts. But you have to stop sooner or later, and then you still have to decide what to do. When Jill stopped, she was very, very thirsty. She had been lying on her face, and now she sat up. The birds had stopped singing, and it was very quiet. But there was one small sound that did not stop. It seemed to come from a good way off. She listened with care, and she was almost sure it was the sound of running water.

paragraphs.context: She had been setting her teeth and clenching her fists for a terrible blast
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Lion’s voice gets softer and Jill goes through the air toward Narnia. His breath is so gentle that she does not know when she leaves the ground.
paragraphs.simple: The voice had been getting softer toward the end of this speech, and now it was gone. Jill looked behind her. She saw that the cliff was already more than a hundred yards behind her, and the Lion himself was a tiny spot of bright gold on the edge of it. She had been holding her teeth together and making her hands into fists, ready for a terrible blast of the Lion’s breath. But the breath had been so gentle that she had not even noticed when she left the ground. And now there was nothing but air for thousands and thousands of feet below her.

paragraphs.context: a little chair on wheels, and, harnessed to it, a little donkey
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jill sees an old, fat Dwarf in a little chair pulled by a little donkey. He is dressed as richly as the King, and his big head is bald.
paragraphs.simple: Right in front of the King there was a little chair with wheels. A little donkey was tied to it, and it was not much bigger than a big retriever dog. The King had turned round to speak to his people before going on board the ship. In the chair sat a fat little Dwarf. He was dressed as richly as the King. But he was fat and sat in a bunch among the cushions, so he looked quite different. He looked like a small shapeless bundle of fur and silk and velvet. He was as old as the King, but stronger and healthier, with very sharp eyes. His head had no hair and was very big. In the light of the sunset it shone like a huge billiard ball.

paragraphs.context: You must get away from here at once. I’ll go and wake
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Owl says there is no time to waste. Jill must leave at once. He will wake the other human, and Jill must change into clothes she can travel in.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Good!’ said the Owl. ‘Then there is no time to lose. You must get away from here at once. I will go and wake the other human. Then I will come back for you. You had better change those court clothes and put on something you can travel in. I will be back very soon. Tu-whoo!’ And without waiting for an answer, he was gone.

paragraphs.context: She had been a great lady, wise and gracious and happy
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Queen has died, and all Narnia is sad. Prince Rilian rides in the north to hunt for the poison worm that killed her, and after a month people see a change in him.
paragraphs.simple: They took the dead Queen back to Cair Paravel. Rilian and the King and all Narnia were very sad. She had been a great lady, wise and kind and happy. She was King Caspian’s bride, whom he had brought home from the east end of the world. People said that she had star blood in her. The Prince took his mother’s death very hard, as well he might. After that he was always riding in the north of Narnia, looking for the poison worm that killed her, to kill it. No one said much about this. The Prince came home from these trips looking tired and upset. But about a month after the Queen’s death, some people said they could see a change in him. There was a look in his eyes like a man who has seen visions. He was out all day, but his horse did not look as if it had been ridden hard. His chief friend among the older men at court was Lord Drinian, who had been his father’s captain on the great trip to the east.

paragraphs.context: Jill had to pinch herself to keep awake, for she knew that if
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jill is so tired that she nearly sleeps on the Owl’s back. At last she gets down and calls Puddleglum.
paragraphs.simple: Jill had to pinch herself to stay awake. She knew that if she slept on Glimfeather’s back, she would probably fall off. At last the two owls stopped flying. She climbed down from Glimfeather, stiff from the ride, and found herself on flat ground. A cold wind was blowing, and there seemed to be no trees. ‘Tu-whoo, tu-whoo!’ called Glimfeather. ‘Wake up, Puddleglum. Wake up. It is the Lion’s business.’

paragraphs.context: Those eels will take a mortal long time to cook
paragraphs.mainIdea: Puddleglum says the eels will take a long time to cook. He will not tell a sad story, so he talks about plans to keep their minds off food.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Now,’ said Puddleglum. ‘Those eels will take a very long time to cook, and one of you might faint from hunger before they are ready. I knew a little girl once. But I had better not tell you that story. It might make you sad, and I never do that. So, to take your minds off your hunger, we may as well talk about our plans.’

paragraphs.context: That night they bivouacked on the bare moor
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children and Puddleglum sleep on the cold hard ground. Puddleglum says it will be colder later, which does not help.
paragraphs.simple: That night they slept in the open on the bare moor. Puddleglum showed the children how to make the best use of their blankets by sleeping back to back. Your backs keep each other warm, and then you can have both blankets on top. But it was still cold, and the ground was hard and not flat. The Marsh-wiggle told them they would feel better if they thought how much colder it would be later and farther north. But this did not cheer them up at all.

paragraphs.context: THERE IS NO DENYING IT WAS A BEAST OF A DAY
paragraphs.mainIdea: The weather is terrible. It is cold, there is snow in the clouds, and the road is broken.
paragraphs.simple: No one can say it was not a terrible day. Above them was a sky with no sun, covered with clouds heavy with snow. On the ground was a black frost. And a wind blew over it that felt as if it would take your skin off. When they came down into the plain, they found that this part of the old road was in much worse shape than any they had seen. They had to find their way over large broken stones, and between big rocks, and across small broken stones. It was hard going for sore feet. And, however tired they got, it was much too cold to stop.

paragraphs.context: I hope you won’t lose all interest in Jill for the rest
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jill cries because she is cold and tired. Crying helps her at that moment.
paragraphs.simple: I hope you will not stop caring about Jill for the rest of the book if I tell you that at this time she began to cry. She had good reasons. Her feet and hands and ears and nose were only just starting to get warm again. Melted snow was running off her clothes. She had had almost nothing to eat or drink that day. Her legs hurt so much that she felt she could not stand much longer. Anyway, it did her more good than anything else would have done, because the Queen said:

paragraphs.context: At lunchtime something happened which made all three of them more anxious
paragraphs.mainIdea: At lunch something happens that makes all three travelers want even more to leave the castle of the Gentle Giants.
paragraphs.simple: At lunch, something happened. It made all three of them want even more to leave the castle of the Gentle Giants. They had lunch in the great hall at a little table of their own, near the fire. At a bigger table, about twenty yards away, six old giants were having lunch. They were so noisy, and their voices were so high in the air, that the children soon paid no more attention to them than you would to car horns outside the window or street noises. They were eating cold deer meat. Jill had never tasted it before, and she liked it.

paragraphs.context: It was pitch black in there, except for the gray light in the opening
paragraphs.mainIdea: The three hide in a cave and fill the opening with stones. The dogs come, and the cave is soon dark.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Quick, quick. Stones. Fill the opening,’ said Puddleglum’s voice in the dark beside her. It was very dark in there, except for the gray light in the opening where they had crawled in. The other two were working hard. She could see Scrubb’s small hands and the Marsh-wiggle’s big hands, black against the light. They were working fast to put stones in a pile. Then she understood how important this was. She looked for large stones herself and gave them to the others. Before the dogs were at the mouth of the cave, they had it nearly full. And now there was no light at all.

paragraphs.context: At last their ship was brought alongside a quay and made fast
paragraphs.mainIdea: The three travelers are taken to a sad city of Earthmen. The Earthmen are busy and no one is interested in them.
paragraphs.simple: At last their ship came to a stop beside a quay (a place for ships) and was tied there. The three travelers were taken to land and marched up into the City. Crowds of Earthmen, no two the same, pushed against them in the busy streets. The sad light fell on many sad and strange faces. But no one showed any interest in the strangers. Every gnome seemed to be as busy as it was sad. Jill never found out what they were so busy about. But the endless moving, pushing and hurrying and the soft pad-pad-pad went on.

paragraphs.context: the heavy, tangled, cold, clammy web of evil magic
paragraphs.mainIdea: The Knight speaks about the magic that holds him. He remembers a pool above ground with trees and sky in it.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Ah,’ he groaned. ‘Spells, spells. A heavy, tangled, cold, wet net of evil magic. Buried alive. Pulled down under the earth, down into the black dark. How many years is it? Have I lived ten years, or a thousand years, in the pit? Maggotmen all around me. Oh, have mercy. Let me out, let me go back. Let me feel the wind and see the sky. There used to be a little pool. When you looked down into it, you could see all the trees growing upside down in the water, all green, and under them, very deep, the blue sky.’

paragraphs.context: the sweet, heavy smell grew very much less
paragraphs.mainIdea: Part of the fire is put out. The sweet smell gets weaker, and the smell of burnt Marsh-wiggle makes everyone think more clearly.
paragraphs.simple: First, the sweet, heavy smell became much less. The whole fire had not been put out, but a good part of it had. What was left smelled mostly of burnt Marsh-wiggle. That is not a nice smell at all. At once everyone’s head was much clearer. The Prince and the children held up their heads again and opened their eyes.

paragraphs.context: it had begun and increased so gradually that they did not know when
paragraphs.mainIdea: A noise grew so slowly that nobody knew when it started. It became a loud roar.
paragraphs.simple: They had all been hearing the noise, but it had started and grown so slowly that they did not know when they first noticed it. For a time it was only a faint, uneasy sound like gentle winds, or like traffic very far away. Then it grew to a low sound like the sea. Then came deep rolling sounds and rushing sounds. Now there seemed to be voices too, and also a steady roar that was not voices.

paragraphs.context: It would have been nasty enough at the bottom even five minutes later
paragraphs.mainIdea: The riders gallop down into a valley where water is rising. They get across just in time.
paragraphs.simple: ‘Hurry,’ cried the Prince. They rode fast down the slope. It would have been bad enough at the bottom even five minutes later. The tide was running up the valley like a fast stream, and if it had come to swimming, the horses could hardly have got across. But the water was still only a foot or two deep. It splashed terribly round the horses’ legs, but they reached the other side safely.

paragraphs.context: She was already in the middle of a crowd when she said this
paragraphs.mainIdea: Many Narnian animals run to Jill. The last to come is a great Panther.
paragraphs.simple: She was already in the middle of a crowd when she said this. Besides the dancers, all kinds of people who had been watching the dance, and whom she had not seen at first, came running up. Squirrels came out of the trees in great numbers, and so did Owls. Hedgehogs came walking from side to side as fast as their short legs could carry them. Bears and Badgers came more slowly. A great Panther, moving its tail in excitement, was the last to join the party.

paragraphs.context: You cannot want wrong things any more, now that you have died, my son
paragraphs.mainIdea: Aslan tells Caspian that he can see the world of Jill and Eustace for five minutes. In that time he can put things right.
paragraphs.simple: ‘You cannot want wrong things any more, now that you have died, my son,’ said Aslan. ‘And you will see their world for five minutes of their time. It will take no longer than that for you to put things right there.’ Then Aslan told Caspian what Jill and Eustace were going back to, and all about Experiment House. He seemed to know it as well as they did.

sentences.context: Nobody asked you to come barging in, did they?
sentences.simple: No one asked you to push in like that, did they?
sentences.grammar: ‘did they?’ is a tag question: after a negative sentence (‘Nobody asked’) it takes a positive tag, and Jill does not want an answer, she wants him to agree he was wrong to come.

sentences.context: The voice had been growing softer toward the end of this speech
sentences.simple: The voice had been getting softer toward the end of this speech, and now it was gone.
sentences.grammar: ‘had been growing’ (past perfect continuous) says the change went on up to ‘now’ in the story, when the voice ‘faded away’.

sentences.context: She had been setting her teeth and clenching her fists for a terrible blast
sentences.simple: She had been holding her teeth together and making her hands into fists for a terrible blast of the Lion’s breath. But the breath had been so gentle that she did not even notice when she left the ground.
sentences.grammar: ‘had been setting … for’ (past perfect continuous) shows she had been getting ready before she looked back; ‘so gentle that’ shows the result.

sentences.context: ought to have been expecting, but which came as a surprise and a shock
sentences.simple: She came out lower than she went in. As soon as she did, she noticed something that she should have expected, but it still came as a surprise and a shock.
sentences.grammar: ‘ought to have been expecting’ means she should have expected it, but did not; the two ‘which’ clauses give two facts about the same thing.

sentences.context: It never occurred to Jill to disbelieve the Lion
sentences.simple: Jill never thought of not believing the Lion. No one who had seen his stern face could do that. And her mind suddenly made itself up.
sentences.grammar: ‘It occurred to Jill to + verb’ means the idea came to her; with ‘never’ it means she had no doubt; the dashes add a reason.

sentences.context: The sun which had been high overhead when she began her journey
sentences.simple: The sun had been high above her when she began her trip. Now it was getting into her eyes.
sentences.grammar: ‘had been’ (past perfect) shows the earlier time when the sun was high; ‘now getting’ shows the later time; ‘which’ adds more about the sun.

sentences.context: A little Faun who had been standing quietly beside the Dwarf
sentences.simple: A little Faun had been standing quietly beside the Dwarf’s elbow all this time. Now he handed the Dwarf a silver ear-trumpet.
sentences.grammar: ‘who had been standing’ (past perfect continuous) shows what the Faun was doing before he handed over the trumpet; ‘now handed’ is the new action.

sentences.context: It was made like the musical instrument called a serpent
sentences.simple: It was made like the musical instrument called a serpent, so that the tube went right round the Dwarf’s neck.
sentences.grammar: ‘It was made’ is passive (who made it is not said); ‘so that’ tells the result of the shape.

sentences.context: who was just gathering up the reins of his donkey
sentences.simple: Before she had time to ask any questions, they had reached the Dwarf. He was just taking up the reins of his donkey, ready to drive back to the castle.
sentences.grammar: ‘who was just gathering’ (past continuous) shows he was in the middle of the action when they came; ‘before she had time to’ shows she had no time.

sentences.context: whom everyone is a little afraid of and everyone makes fun of
sentences.simple: The Narnians felt about Trumpkin as people at school feel about an old teacher who is not kind. Everyone is a little afraid of him and makes fun of him, but nobody really dislikes him.
sentences.grammar: One ‘whom’ clause covers three actions (afraid of, makes fun of, dislikes); ‘of’ stays at the end, so ‘afraid of whom’ becomes ‘whom … afraid of’.

sentences.context: She had been a great lady, wise and gracious and happy
sentences.simple: She had been a great lady, wise and kind and happy. She was King Caspian’s bride, whom he had brought home from the east end of the world.
sentences.grammar: ‘had been’ and ‘had brought’ (past perfect) look back at her life before the story’s time; ‘whom he had brought’ adds more about the bride.

sentences.context: that the parliament had been going on quite long enough
sentences.simple: One or two owls added that even here in the ruined tower it was not nearly so dark as when they began, and that the meeting had gone on long enough.
sentences.grammar: After ‘added that’ the speech moves back one tense: ‘had been going on’ (past perfect continuous) says the meeting had lasted a long time; ‘not so dark as’ compares two times.

sentences.context: Jill had to pinch herself to keep awake, for she knew that if
sentences.simple: Jill had to pinch herself to stay awake, because she knew that if she slept on Glimfeather’s back, she would probably fall off.
sentences.grammar: ‘she knew that if she dozed …, she would probably fall’ is a thought in the past: ‘would’ is the past of ‘will’ and tells what could happen; ‘for’ means ‘because’.

sentences.context: Scrubb had brought the one which had been left out for him
sentences.simple: Scrubb had brought the sword that someone had left out for him in his room at Cair Paravel. But Jill had to be happy with her knife.
sentences.grammar: ‘which had been left out’ is passive past perfect: someone left it earlier; ‘had to be content with’ means she had to accept less.

sentences.context: The others must give an absolute promise that, unless he gave them leave
sentences.simple: The others must promise that, unless he said they could, they would not tell the Gentle Giants that they came from Narnia or that they were looking for Prince Rilian.
sentences.grammar: ‘unless’ means ‘if not’; ‘gave them leave’ means ‘gave them permission’; ‘would not tell’ is the promise, reported in the past.

sentences.context: first of those quarrels which Puddleglum had foretold
sentences.simple: Now they nearly had the first of those quarrels that Puddleglum had said would come. Jill and Scrubb had often snapped at each other before, but this was the first really serious disagreement.
sentences.grammar: ‘had foretold’ (past perfect) says he spoke before it happened; ‘not that … hadn’t been sparring’ says that small fights had happened before.

sentences.context: were absolutely dead set to visit the Gentle Giants
sentences.simple: The children were sick of wind and rain, thin birds cooked over campfires, and hard, cold ground to sleep on. They very much wanted to visit the Gentle Giants.
sentences.grammar: ‘The children, … who were sick of …, were … dead set’: the ‘who’ clause between commas gives the reason; ‘on the other hand’ contrasts them with Puddleglum; ‘dead set to + verb’ means very sure they want to do it.

sentences.context: In order to understand what followed, you must keep on remembering
sentences.simple: To understand what came next, you must keep on remembering how little they could see.
sentences.grammar: ‘In order to + verb’ tells the purpose; ‘what followed’ is a noun clause meaning ‘the things that came next’; ‘keep on + -ing’ means do it again and again.

sentences.context: they could not have heard him even if they had wanted to
sentences.simple: The Marsh-wiggle followed them, still talking. But they were pushing against the wind again, so they could not have heard him, even if they had wanted to.
sentences.grammar: ‘could not have heard … even if they had wanted to’ is about the past: ‘could not have + verb’ says it was impossible, and ‘even if’ + past perfect says that wanting would not change it.

sentences.context: a wind that felt as if it would take your skin off
sentences.simple: Above them was a sky with no sun, covered with clouds heavy with snow. On the ground was a black frost. And a wind blew over it that felt as if it would take your skin off.
sentences.grammar: The sentence is a list of three phrases with no verb until the last; ‘as if it would’ compares the wind to something that is not real.

sentences.context: Puddleglum was dead against any idea of telling the giants their real business
sentences.simple: Puddleglum was very much against any idea of telling the giants why they had really come and just asking to be let out. The children could not tell without his permission, because they had promised.
sentences.grammar: ‘dead against + any idea of + -ing’ means strongly against doing it; ‘because they had promised’ gives an earlier reason.

sentences.context: A few minutes ago when they had been in the kitchen
sentences.simple: A few minutes before, in the kitchen, she had thought that if only they could once get out of the castle, their escape would be almost complete. Now she saw that the most dangerous part was still to come.
sentences.grammar: ‘if only … could’ shows a strong wish; ‘would be’ is a past thought about the future; ‘was still to come’ means it had not happened yet.

sentences.context: Suddenly Puddleglum turned to them, and his face had gone so pale
sentences.simple: Puddleglum suddenly turned to them. His face had gone so pale that you could see the paleness under the natural muddy color of his skin.
sentences.grammar: ‘had gone so pale that …’ shows a result; ‘go’ + adjective means ‘become’, and the past perfect says the change was finished before he turned.

sentences.context: which must have been a long way overhead
sentences.simple: The light was not strong enough to reach the roof of the cave, which must have been very far above them.
sentences.grammar: ‘must have been’ (modal + perfect) is a strong guess about the past: they think it is true but cannot see; the ‘which’ clause adds more about the roof.

sentences.context: (WHICH WAS PIGEON PIE, COLD ham, salad, and cakes) had been brought
sentences.simple: When the meal (pigeon pie, cold ham, salad and cakes) had been brought, and all had pulled their chairs up to the table and begun, the Knight went on.
sentences.grammar: ‘had been brought’ is passive past perfect: the food came first, then the Knight spoke; the words in brackets give extra detail about the meal.

sentences.context: his own sword (which had been taken from him and laid on the table)
sentences.simple: As soon as the prisoner was free, he jumped across the room in one bound, took his own sword and drew it. Someone had taken the sword from him and put it on the table.
sentences.grammar: ‘which had been taken … and laid’ is a passive past perfect ‘which’ clause: it says what had been done to the sword before; the three verbs (crossed, seized, drew) are quick steps.

sentences.context: that they tunnel not a score of feet beneath the very grass
sentences.simple: Her Earthmen have worked day and night to dig a way under it. They have now come so far and so high that their tunnel is less than twenty feet under the grass where the people of that country walk.
sentences.grammar: ‘not a score of feet’ means ‘less than twenty feet’ (a score is twenty); ‘tunnel’ is used as a verb; ‘so far and so high that’ shows a result.

sentences.context: the great serpent which the Witch had become, green as poison
sentences.simple: The Witch had become a great snake, green as poison and as thick as Jill’s waist. Before anyone had time to do anything, it had thrown two or three coils of its horrible body round the Prince’s legs.
sentences.grammar: ‘which the Witch had become’ is a ‘which’ clause in the past perfect: she changed first, then the snake ‘had flung’ its coils; ‘as poison’ and ‘as Jill’s waist’ are comparisons.

sentences.context: whom some call Caspian the Seafarer
sentences.simple: I am Rilian, the King’s son of Narnia. I am the only child of Caspian, Tenth of that name, whom some call Caspian the Seafarer.
sentences.grammar: ‘Tenth of that name’ means the tenth king called Caspian; ‘whom some call …’ is a ‘whom’ clause, where ‘whom’ is the object of ‘call’.

sentences.context: you can put nothing into your make-believe without copying it
sentences.simple: Look: you cannot put anything into your make-believe without copying it from the real world, this world of mine, which is the only world.
sentences.grammar: ‘nothing … without + -ing’ means that every time you put something in, you copy it; the last ‘which’ clause adds a claim about the real world.

sentences.context: They had all, in fact, been hearing the noise but it had begun
sentences.simple: They had all been hearing the noise. But it had started and grown so slowly that they did not know when they first noticed it.
sentences.grammar: ‘had been hearing’ (past perfect continuous) says they heard it for some time before they noticed; ‘so gradually that’ shows a result.

sentences.context: The Witch had locked the door and told the Earthmen not to disturb her
sentences.simple: The Witch had locked the door and told the Earthmen not to disturb her. So for now there was no danger that anyone would stop them.
sentences.grammar: ‘told the Earthmen not to + verb’ is a reported order (a negative command); the past perfect puts it before the time of the story.

sentences.context: would have thought Golg had sent them the wrong way if they
sentences.simple: They would have thought Golg had sent them the wrong way if they had not seen, on the other side of the valley, the lamps going on and up as far as they could see.
sentences.grammar: Third conditional: ‘would have thought … if they had not seen’ is about the past; they did see the lamps, so they did not think they were lost.

sentences.context: and if it had come to swimming, the horses could hardly have won over
sentences.simple: The tide was running up the valley like a fast stream. If it had come to swimming, the horses could hardly have got across.
sentences.grammar: ‘if it had come to swimming’ (past perfect) means ‘if swimming had been needed’, and ‘could hardly have got across’ says it was almost impossible; both talk about something that did not happen.

sentences.context: all sorts of people who had been watching the dance, and whom
sentences.simple: All kinds of people who had been watching the dance, and whom she had not seen at first, came running up.
sentences.grammar: ‘who had been watching’ (past perfect continuous) and ‘whom she had not seen’ are two clauses that tell more about ‘people’ before they came running.

sentences.context: So that when he had persuaded Puddleglum to give him a back
sentences.simple: So when he had talked Puddleglum into giving him a back, and drawn his sword, and put out his head, he had really been doing a very brave thing.
sentences.grammar: ‘when he had persuaded …, and drawn …, and poked out …’ lists three steps in the past perfect; the main clause ‘he had really been doing’ says all of this together was a brave act.

sentences.context: Eustace tackled it just as if he had not had a very large supper
sentences.simple: Breakfast was scrambled eggs and toast. Eustace ate it just as if he had not had a very big supper in the middle of the night.
sentences.grammar: ‘just as if he had not had’ (past perfect) compares to something that was not true: he had eaten a lot; ‘tackled’ means he attacked the food hungrily.

sentences.context: Puddleglum (whose foot was as good as new in three weeks) often pointed out
sentences.simple: Rilian ruled Narnia well, and the land was happy in his days. But Puddleglum (whose foot was as good as new in three weeks) often said that bright mornings are followed by wet afternoons, and that you could not expect good times to last.
sentences.grammar: ‘whose foot’ is a ‘whose’ clause in brackets, meaning ‘the foot of Puddleglum’; ‘though’ contrasts the happy land with Puddleglum’s warnings; ‘as good as new’ is a comparison.
